title: The call is the answer
hookLine: a man stops calling on God because no answer comes, and learns his calling was itself the answer (Masnavi 3.189ff)
carry: the wanting is the answer, arriving

cards: You text someone. Two blue ticks, and nothing. You text again the next day.
Nothing. By the third try, a little voice says: why are you still doing this? They're not answering.
Stop embarrassing yourself. Plenty of people feel that way about prayer, or meditation, or any practice that doesn't send back a receipt. You keep showing up, and the sky stays quiet.
Rumi tells a story about a man who heard that same little voice, and listened to it.

teach.b: It's in Book Three of the Masnavi. A man is calling on God through the night: Allah, Allah, over and over, until his lips grow sweet with it. And the devil, in Rumi's telling, comes with a very reasonable question.
All this calling, and where's the reply? Where's the here I am from God?
Not one answer is coming back. How long will you keep this up? The man's heart breaks.
He stops, lies down and falls asleep. And in a dream he sees Khidr, the mysterious guide of Islamic tradition. Why have you stopped calling on God?
Khidr asks. Do you regret it? The man says: no answer ever came.
I'm afraid I've been turned away from the door. And Khidr gives him God's reply. Your calling Allah is my here I am.

teach.h: YOUR CALL IS MY HERE I AM.
teach.b: Your longing, your pleading, your ache, those are my messengers to you. The very pull that made you call was me, drawing you. Beneath every O Lord of yours are many here I am's from me.

The man thought his call went up and the answer should come down, like a text and its reply. Rumi says it's already the other way round. In his telling, the longing comes from the one being longed for.

Rumi is talking about God, and not everyone listening prays. But the idea travels: sometimes the fact that you keep showing up is the thing you were waiting for. Your line: the wanting is the answer, arriving.

how: People who pray, in many traditions, describe times when prayer feels unanswered; in Sufi teaching this story is read as a comfort for those times, saying the longing itself is a gift from God.

a hidden guide who comes to the man in a dream
an angel who writes down each prayer you make

labbayk, the reply the man wanted

he stopped because no answer came and he feared he'd been turned away.
in the dream, God's reply says the calling itself is 'here I am'
your calling Allah is my here I am, the story says.
Khidr appears in the story to bring the reply
the mysterious guide of Islamic tradition comes to him in a dream.

games.q: you've called on God all night, and a voice asks: where's the answer? not one reply has come. what does the man do?
o: stop calling, and fall asleep broken-hearted.
games.why: he stops and falls asleep, and in a dream Khidr tells him his calling was God's answer all along.

practice: Settle into this sit the way the man settled into his calling, with no result expected. If you pray, you can pray, and let it be enough that you're praying; if you don't, just sit, and let it be enough that you're sitting.
When a voice asks what the point is, notice it, and keep going.

wordCard.voice: Khidr. The mysterious guide who appears to the man in a dream and tells him his very calling on God was already God's reply. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic, used in Persian: 'here I am', the answer to a call: the reply the man was waiting for.

carryVoice: Your line: the wanting is the answer, arriving. In Rumi's telling, the longing was never one-way. Day two hundred three.

sources.ref: Masnavi 3.189ff (the man who called 'Allah' and received no answer)
